---
title: "Accessible Maths: a first interactive theorem"
filters: [accessible-maths]
format:
  html: default
  docx: default
---

This tutorial uses ordinary Quarto mathematics and author-written content. Start
with the theorem and proof, make one change, then try the optional explanations.
It needs no knowledge catalogue, AI model or experimental maths engine.

## 1. Render and open a proof

In this source folder, open `example.qmd` and use your editor's **Render** or
**Preview** command. From a terminal you can instead run:

```sh
quarto render example.qmd --to html
```

If working in another folder, first follow the installation instructions in
`README.md` and copy this file there. A GitHub installation uses
`filters: [kai-prince-sfhea/accessible-maths]`; the local installation used by
this article uses `filters: [accessible-maths]`.

The rendered result should show the numbered theorem below and a closed
**Proof** disclosure. Select **Proof** to reveal the argument, then follow
**Back to statement**. You can also focus the disclosure with Tab and open it
with Enter or Space.

::: {#thm-positive-square name="Positive squares"}
For every non-zero real number $x$, the square $x^2$ is positive.
:::

::: {#prf-positive-square .proof proof-for="#thm-positive-square"}
If $x>0$, the product $x\cdot x$ is positive. If $x<0$, then $-x>0$
and $x\cdot x=(-x)\cdot(-x)>0$.
:::

The statement uses Quarto's native `thm-` identifier. The proof's `proof-for`
attribute points to that statement; no word matching or inferred association is
involved. Native references such as @thm-positive-square still work.

## 2. Change one label and render again

In the source, add `am-summary="Proof by signs"` to the proof's opening line:

```markdown
::: {#prf-positive-square .proof proof-for="#thm-positive-square" am-summary="Proof by signs"}
```

Render again. The proof's disclosure label and its link beneath the theorem
should now read **Proof by signs**. You changed the interface label; the
statement and its authored proof are still the same text.

## 3. Try an authored hint and assumption

The next two blocks already have explicit associations and meaningful labels.
Open them in the preview, then edit their text or summaries in the source and
render again. Keep each summary distinct when several blocks refer to the same
statement.

::: {#hint-sign .am-hint theorem-for="#thm-positive-square" am-summary="Hint: consider both signs"}
Consider the positive and negative cases separately.
:::

::: {#assumption-real .am-assumption theorem-for="#thm-positive-square" am-summary="Assumption: a non-zero real input"}
The statement concerns non-zero elements of the ordered field of real numbers.
:::

## 4. Try two explanation levels

An explanation needs its own summary. Giving explanations distinct `am-level`
values adds an **Explanation level** selector beneath the associated theorem.
Return to the theorem and choose **Introductory**, then **Advanced**, then
**All explanations**. Only these authored explanations are filtered; the
statement, proof, hint and assumption remain available.

::: {#explanation-intro .am-explanation theorem-for="#thm-positive-square" am-summary="Intuitive explanation" am-level="Introductory"}
Two positive factors give a positive product. Two negative factors also give
a positive product. The non-zero condition excludes a square of zero.
:::

::: {#explanation-advanced .am-explanation theorem-for="#thm-positive-square" am-summary="Explanation using order axioms" am-level="Advanced"}
In the ordered field of real numbers, either $x>0$ or $-x>0$ when $x\ne0$.
The product of two positive elements is positive, and $(-x)^2=x^2$.
:::

[Jump directly to the introductory explanation](#explanation-intro) to see its
containing disclosure open. The extension retains all authored bodies when you
print or render this article to Word:

```sh
quarto render example.qmd --to docx
```

## 5. Try one optional notation exercise

You can keep the ordinary setup above. To try a definition that supplies its
notation once, copy the following block into the end of your own article, then
render it:

```markdown
::: {#def-power name="Power notation" semantic-id="https://example.org/maths/power" am-macro="amPower" am-args="base exponent" am-optional="base" am-default="2" am-intent="power($base,$exponent)" am-tex="#1^{#2}"}
The first argument is the base and the second is the exponent.
:::

The default is $\amPower{3}$; an explicit base is $\amPower[5]{3}$.
```

The two expressions should show two cubed and five cubed. Change the default
from `2` to `4` and render again: only the omitted-base expression changes.
The exercise uses ordinary visual mathematics; it does not need the experimental
MathJax configuration. The README explains additional signatures, local scopes
and separately reviewed catalogue/speech options.

## 6. Choose your next step

Use `README.md` for label translation, YAML options, appearance hooks and
companion-extension behaviour. You can keep this setup when composing a page
from normal Quarto includes; associations resolve on the resulting page.

For the separate `intent`/`arg` annotation experiment, open and render
`advanced.qmd`. That file deliberately selects the pinned experimental MathJax
engine. Nothing in this tutorial requires that experiment.

The synthetic mathematics and explanations are author-written examples, not
proof-verification or accessibility-conformance results. Review the meaning and
accessibility of your own material before publishing.
